title: Build a polite mini SEO site auditor in Python with robots.txt and a tiny crawl
summary:
Commercial SEO crawlers are excellent. You do not need one of them to learn the pattern: read robots.txt, fetch a few pages politely, measure a handful of on-page signals, and write the findings somewhere a human can act on.

In this tutorial we build a small, polite Python script that:

  1. reads robots.txt and stops if User-agent: * (and our bot) may not fetch the start URL,
  2. crawls a tiny site breadth-first with hard caps (pages, depth, timeout, body size),
  3. per page records title / meta description length, H1 count, canonical, meta robots / X-Robots-Tag, basic Open Graph presence, images missing alt, internal vs external link counts, HTTP status and redirect hops,
  4. checks a few broken internal links only (HEAD, with GET fallback),
  5. reads whether robots.txt names common AI crawlers (GPTBot, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, …) — read rules only, never impersonate those bots,
  6. optionally probes for llms.txt and sitemap.xml,
  7. writes CSV and JSON, and attaches a simple 0–100 score with plain-English fix hints.

Dependencies: Python 3.9+ (tested on 3.13) and requests. HTML and robots parsing use the standard library. The full script is at the end. Every figure below comes from live runs on 6 November 2026.

The checks are a small educational subset. They are incomplete on purpose. Treat them as teaching examples, not as a product rule catalogue.

Why pure Python (and only requests)

There is nothing wrong with Playwright, Scrapy or a hosted auditor. For a tutorial, a single file you can read top to bottom beats a framework:

  • urllib.robotparser and html.parser are in the standard library.
  • requests handles TLS, redirects and a session cookie jar without ceremony.
  • Hard caps (pages, depth, bytes, link-check budget) keep the script safe to point at a stranger's documentation site once.
  • You can paste the script into a throwaway venv and delete it when you are done.

If you later move the same ideas into an async service, keep the politeness contract: robots first, clear User-Agent, rate limit, capped bodies, no personal data.

What we will not do

  • Crawl a whole production site. Default caps are 10 pages and depth 2.
  • Log in, solve captchas, rotate proxies or ignore Disallow.
  • Harvest mailto: / tel: links, form contents or anything that looks like a person.
  • Send User-Agent: GPTBot (or any other third-party bot name) to see what happens. We only read those rules from robots.txt.
  • Pitch a hosted product. This is a standalone script you can read and run.

One site, several layers of signal

Take crawlee.dev from the live run on 6 November 2026. After robots.txt allowed our bot and *, an eight-page crawl (depth ≤ 2) returned:

Layer What showed up
Homepage HTTP 200, title 40 chars, meta description 146 chars, one H1, self-canonical, Open Graph present, score 100
Site extras sitemap.xml declared in robots and present; llms.txt HTTP 200
Deeper pages Blog title 107 chars (soft-max notice); a couple of JS/Python pages with images missing alt
Roll-up Average score 97.8 across 8 pages; no broken internal links in the sample

That mix is the point of the exercise. A homepage that scores 100 can still sit next to a blog index with a long title and no H1. A useful mini auditor shows both — still with a tiny crawl budget.

Step 1: be a polite bot

Identify yourself. The educational User-Agent in this tutorial is:

LindenwerkDataEducationalBot/0.1 (+https://dev.to/lindenwerkdata; educational tiny SEO site-audit tutorial; honours robots.txt)

Then honour RFC 9309-style robots rules with urllib.robotparser. The script fetches /robots.txt first (capped body size). Practical rules we use:

  • HTTP 404 / other 4xx on robots.txt → treat as no rules, allow the fetch (common convention; example.com returned 404 in our run and we continued).
  • HTTP 5xx on robots.txt → treat as disallow (conservative).
  • Otherwise parse the file and require both our bot name and User-agent: * to be allowed for the URL we are about to request.
  • Every later page and internal link check goes through the same parser.

On 6 November 2026, crawlee.dev and docs.python.org served normal robots files that allow / for * and our bot. A unit check of RobotFileParser with Disallow: / correctly returns False for /.

from urllib.parse import urlsplit, urlunsplit
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser

def robots_allows(session, page_url):
    parts = urlsplit(page_url)
    robots_url = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, "/robots.txt", "", ""))
    r = session.get(robots_url, timeout=15, stream=True)
    # ... read a capped body ...
    if 400 <= r.status_code < 500:
        return True, f"robots.txt {r.status_code} (no rules → allow)"
    if r.status_code >= 500:
        return False, f"robots.txt {r.status_code} (treat as disallow)"
    rp = RobotFileParser()
    rp.parse(body.decode("utf-8", "replace").splitlines())
    target = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, parts.path or "/", parts.query, ""))
    allowed = rp.can_fetch("LindenwerkDataEducationalBot", target) and rp.can_fetch("*", target)
    return allowed, "robots.txt OK"

If robots say no, the site row is stored as robots_disallowed and no HTML crawl is started.

Step 2: a tiny breadth-first crawl 

from collections import deque

queue = deque([(start_url, 0)])
seen = set()
while queue and len(pages) < max_pages:
    url, depth = queue.popleft()
    if url in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(url)
    if not robots_allows_url(robots, url):
        continue
    # GET with timeout + 1 MB body cap, then parse …
    if depth < max_depth:
        for href in internal_hrefs:
            queue.append((href, depth + 1))

Defaults in the script: 10 pages, depth 2, 0.75 s pause between requests, 15 s timeout, 1 MB HTML cap. Query strings are stripped when discovering new URLs (keeps the frontier small). Static asset extensions (.png, .css, .js, …) are skipped. mailto: and tel: are never followed.

Live on 6 November 2026 with --max-pages 8 --max-depth 2:

  • example.com → 1 page (no further internal links)
  • crawlee.dev → 8 pages
  • docs.python.org → 8 pages
  • httpbin.org → 2 pages

Step 3: per-page on-page checks

An HTMLParser subclass collects </code>, meta tags, H1 count, <code>rel=canonical</code>, Open Graph keys, image <code>alt</code> presence and anchor <code>href</code>s — without walking <code>mailto:</code> / <code>tel:</code>.</p> <p>For each page the script records:</p> <div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table> <thead> <tr> <th>Signal</th> <th>How we treat it (educational soft targets)</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>HTTP status / redirects</td> <td>4xx/5xx = error; ≥2 redirect hops = warning</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Title length</td> <td>missing = error; < 30 = warning; > 60 = notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Meta description</td> <td>missing = warning; outside ~70–160 = notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td>H1</td> <td>0 = warning; > 1 = notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Canonical</td> <td>missing = notice; cross-domain = warning; self vs other labelled</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Indexability</td> <td> <code>noindex</code> in meta robots or <code>X-Robots-Tag</code> = warning</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Open Graph</td> <td>no <code>og:title</code> / <code>og:description</code> / <code>og:image</code> / <code>og:url</code> = notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Images</td> <td>count of <code><img></code> with missing/empty <code>alt</code> </td> </tr> </tbody> </table></div> <p><code>example.com</code> on 6 November 2026 is a useful teaching case. The live HTML is a short documentation stub: title <strong>"Example Domain"</strong> (14 characters), <strong>no H1</strong>, no meta description, no canonical, no Open Graph. Score <strong>86</strong>. (Older textbook copies of that page had an H1 — the public page changed; the script reports what the network returns today.)</p> <p><code>crawlee.dev/</code> scored <strong>100</strong> on the same day: title 40 chars, description 146, one H1, self-canonical, Open Graph keys present, 14 images all with alt text.</p> <h2> Step 4: a few broken internal links only </h2> <p>Full-site link checking is expensive and easy to abuse. The educational script keeps a small pool of internal URLs discovered during the crawl that were <strong>not</strong> already fetched as pages, then:</p> <ol> <li>skips any URL robots disallow,</li> <li>sends <strong>HEAD</strong> (falls back to a tiny GET if the host rejects HEAD),</li> <li>stops after <code>--max-link-checks</code> (default 15).</li> </ol> <p>Broken samples land on the site row as <code>broken_internal_links</code> and contribute a site-level <code>broken_internal_link</code> issue. On our 6 November 2026 runs across example.com, crawlee.dev, docs.python.org, httpbin.org and cloudflare.com, the sampled internal links all responded OK — which is a fine outcome; the plumbing is what you are learning.</p> <h2> Step 5: read AI-bot rules (do not wear their badges) </h2> <p>Many sites now name AI crawlers explicitly in <code>robots.txt</code>. The script looks for a short list (GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, Anthropic-AI, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, CCBot, …) and, for each:</p> <ul> <li>whether the name appears in the file,</li> <li>whether <code>RobotFileParser.can_fetch(bot_name, homepage)</code> is true,</li> <li>a one-line policy hint.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Important:</strong> page fetches and link checks always use <em>our</em> educational User-Agent. We never send <code>User-Agent: GPTBot</code> to "see what the CDN does". Impersonating another bot is rude, often against terms, and unnecessary for reading a public rules file.</p> <p>On 6 November 2026, <code>cloudflare.com/robots.txt</code> explicitly named GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, Google-Extended, Anthropic-AI, Claude-Web, CCBot, PerplexityBot (and Cohere-ai) with <code>Allow: /</code> for each. The script reported <code>named_in_robots: true</code> and <code>homepage_allowed: true</code> for those entries. <code>crawlee.dev</code> and <code>docs.python.org</code> named none of the AI bots in our teaching list — they fall under <code>User-agent: *</code>.</p> <h2> Step 6: optional <code>llms.txt</code> and sitemap presence </h2> <p>Two cheap HEAD/GET probes (still rate-limited):</p> <ul> <li> <code>/llms.txt</code> — present or not (reported as information; search engines may ignore it).</li> <li>Sitemap — first <code>Sitemap:</code> URL from robots.txt, else <code>/sitemap.xml</code>.</li> </ul> <p>Live on 6 November 2026:</p> <div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table> <thead> <tr> <th>Site</th> <th>Sitemap</th> <th>llms.txt</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>example.com</td> <td>404</td> <td>404</td> </tr> <tr> <td>crawlee.dev</td> <td>200 (from robots)</td> <td>200</td> </tr> <tr> <td>docs.python.org</td> <td>200 (from robots)</td> <td>404</td> </tr> <tr> <td>httpbin.org</td> <td>404</td> <td>404</td> </tr> <tr> <td>cloudflare.com</td> <td>200 (from robots)</td> <td>200</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></div> <h2> Step 7: score, fix hints, CSV and JSON </h2> <p>Each page starts at <strong>100</strong>. Unique issue ids subtract <strong>10</strong> (error), <strong>4</strong> (warning) or <strong>1</strong> (notice). Every issue carries a short <code>fix</code> string a non-engineer can read:<br /> </p> <div class="highlight js-code-highlight"> <pre class="highlight json"><code><span class="p">{</span> <span class="nl">"id"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="s2">"title_short"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nl">"severity"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="s2">"warning"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nl">"message"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="s2">"Title only 14 chars (soft min ~30)"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nl">"fix"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="s2">"Expand the title toward ~30–60 characters without stuffing."</span> <span class="p">}</span> </code></pre> </div> <p>Outputs:</p> <ul> <li> <strong>JSON</strong> — site row (<code>rowType: "site"</code>) plus one page row per URL (<code>rowType: "page"</code>), including the AI-bot matrix and broken-link samples.</li> <li> <strong>CSV</strong> — flat spreadsheet of page metrics plus a <code>[site]</code> summary row with average score and top issue ids.</li> </ul> <p>Soft length targets are teaching defaults, not Google policy quotes. Adjust them for your own style guide.</p> <h2> Limitations you should expect </h2> <ol> <li> <strong>Client-rendered apps</strong> may ship an almost empty HTML shell. A single GET will under-count H1s and text. Headless browsers are out of scope here on purpose.</li> <li> <strong>Soft title/description ranges</strong> are conventions, not guarantees of ranking.</li> <li> <strong>Broken-link sample ≠ full link audit.</strong> Raising <code>--max-link-checks</code> still only samples the frontier; it is not a substitute for a dedicated checker.</li> <li> <strong>AI-bot matrix is a reading aid.</strong> Bot names change; keep the list short and honest.</li> <li> <strong>The rule list is tiny.</strong> Real auditors have dozens of rule types (hreflang, JSON-LD, thin content, mixed content, …). Growing yours is fine — keep evidence, keep caps, keep robots.</li> </ol> <h2> Scheduling a weekly re-audit </h2> <p>Companion file <code>crontab.txt</code>:<br /> </p> <div class="highlight js-code-highlight"> <pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>CRON_TZ=Europe/Berlin 30 7 * * 1 cd /path/to/code && ./venv/bin/python seo_audit.py -f domains.txt --max-pages 10 --max-depth 2 --out-dir out >> out/cron.log 2>&1 </code></pre> </div> <p>Keep <code>max-pages</code> low. A free shared runner is not a reason to hammer strangers. Diff this week's JSON against last week's if you want a change watch — the educational script itself does not ship a state file (unlike a one-page tech detector); a <code>jq</code> diff is enough to start.</p> <h2> Live results (6 November 2026) </h2> <p>Fresh venv, Python 3.13.5, <code>requests</code> 2.32.4. Public sites, educational caps:</p> <div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table> <thead> <tr> <th>Input</th> <th>Pages</th> <th>Avg score</th> <th>robots</th> <th>Notable findings</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>example.com</td> <td>1</td> <td>86.0</td> <td>404 → allow</td> <td>Title 14 chars; no H1 / meta description / canonical / OG; no sitemap / llms.txt</td> </tr> <tr> <td>crawlee.dev</td> <td>8</td> <td>97.8</td> <td>allow</td> <td>Homepage score 100; sitemap + llms.txt present; some long titles / missing alt deeper in</td> </tr> <tr> <td>docs.python.org</td> <td>8</td> <td>95.0</td> <td>allow</td> <td>Many short titles (docs pattern); sitemap present; llms.txt 404</td> </tr> <tr> <td>httpbin.org</td> <td>2</td> <td>83.0</td> <td>allow</td> <td>Homepage short title; <code>/forms/post</code> missing title</td> </tr> <tr> <td>cloudflare.com</td> <td>5</td> <td>95.6</td> <td>allow</td> <td>AI bots explicitly named + allowed; sitemap + llms.txt present</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></div> <p>Outputs from these runs contained <strong>zero</strong> e-mail addresses and <strong>zero</strong> phone numbers. The script never parses <code>mailto:</code> / <code>tel:</code> and never posts forms.</p> <h2> Run it yourself </h2> <div class="highlight js-code-highlight"> <pre class="highlight shell"><code>python3 -m venv venv ./venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt <span class="c"># pins requests</span> ./venv/bin/python seo_audit.py \ example.com crawlee.dev docs.python.org \ --max-pages 10 --max-depth 2 --out-dir out </code></pre> </div> <p>Useful flags: <code>--max-link-checks 15</code>, <code>--no-llms</code>, <code>--no-sitemap</code>, <code>--file domains.txt</code>, <code>--pause 1.0</code>. An example <code>crontab.txt</code> in the companion folder shows a Monday weekly re-audit; it is not installed for you.</p> <h2> Where to take it next </h2> <ul> <li>Feed a CSV of <em>your own</em> sites or client domains and keep the pause (or slower).</li> <li>Raise caps only when you have permission and a reason.</li> <li>Add duplicate-title detection across the small page set you already fetched.</li> <li>Add security-header scoring (HSTS, CSP) as a separate optional block.</li> <li>Export the issues array into a spreadsheet your editor can tick through.</li> <li>For agency lead lists, start from domains you are allowed to review — do not scrape personal contact details to build those lists.</li> </ul> <p>Still a tiny crawl. Still no personal data. Still your script, under your control.</p> <h2> Privacy checklist (short) </h2> <p>Before you point this at someone else's property in bulk:</p> <ol> <li>You have a legitimate reason (your inventory, a client who asked, research you are allowed to do).</li> <li>robots.txt is honoured; a clear bot name is in the User-Agent; requests are rate-limited.</li> <li>Outputs are scanned for e-mails and phone numbers (our live runs: <strong>zero</strong>).</li> <li>Form posts, account areas, <code>mailto:</code> / <code>tel:</code> and cookie <strong>values</strong> are off limits.</li> <li>AI-bot names are read from robots.txt — never sent as the request User-Agent.</li> <li>Soft SEO scores are not sold as a ranking certificate.</li> </ol> <p>That checklist is operational hygiene, not legal advice.</p> <h2> Terms and honesty </h2> <p>Only public HTML, headers and robots.txt are used. Honour robots.txt and site terms. Do not use this pattern to build bulk marketing lists of people. Vendor and bot names (Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Cloudflare, …) are used as factual labels for publicly visible rules and pages; this tutorial is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by those organisations. event_model_payload.headline: Build a polite mini SEO site auditor in Python with robots.txt and a tiny crawl
event_model_payload.summary:
Commercial SEO crawlers are excellent. You do not need one of them to learn the pattern: read robots.txt, fetch a few pages politely, measure a handful of on-page signals, and write the findings somewhere a human can act on.

In this tutorial we build a small, polite Python script that:

  1. reads robots.txt and stops if User-agent: * (and our bot) may not fetch the start URL,
  2. crawls a tiny site breadth-first with hard caps (pages, depth, timeout, body size),
  3. per page records title / meta description length, H1 count, canonical, meta robots / X-Robots-Tag, basic Open Graph presence, images missing alt, internal vs external link counts, HTTP status and redirect hops,
  4. checks a few broken internal links only (HEAD, with GET fallback),
  5. reads whether robots.txt names common AI crawlers (GPTBot, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, …) — read rules only, never impersonate those bots,
  6. optionally probes for llms.txt and sitemap.xml,
  7. writes CSV and JSON, and attaches a simple 0–100 score with plain-English fix hints.

Dependencies: Python 3.9+ (tested on 3.13) and requests. HTML and robots parsing use the standard library. The full script is at the end. Every figure below comes from live runs on 6 November 2026.

The checks are a small educational subset. They are incomplete on purpose. Treat them as teaching examples, not as a product rule catalogue.

Why pure Python (and only requests)

There is nothing wrong with Playwright, Scrapy or a hosted auditor. For a tutorial, a single file you can read top to bottom beats a framework:

  • urllib.robotparser and html.parser are in the standard library.
  • requests handles TLS, redirects and a session cookie jar without ceremony.
  • Hard caps (pages, depth, bytes, link-check budget) keep the script safe to point at a stranger's documentation site once.
  • You can paste the script into a throwaway venv and delete it when you are done.

If you later move the same ideas into an async service, keep the politeness contract: robots first, clear User-Agent, rate limit, capped bodies, no personal data.

What we will not do

  • Crawl a whole production site. Default caps are 10 pages and depth 2.
  • Log in, solve captchas, rotate proxies or ignore Disallow.
  • Harvest mailto: / tel: links, form contents or anything that looks like a person.
  • Send User-Agent: GPTBot (or any other third-party bot name) to see what happens. We only read those rules from robots.txt.
  • Pitch a hosted product. This is a standalone script you can read and run.

One site, several layers of signal

Take crawlee.dev from the live run on 6 November 2026. After robots.txt allowed our bot and *, an eight-page crawl (depth ≤ 2) returned:

Layer What showed up
Homepage HTTP 200, title 40 chars, meta description 146 chars, one H1, self-canonical, Open Graph present, score 100
Site extras sitemap.xml declared in robots and present; llms.txt HTTP 200
Deeper pages Blog title 107 chars (soft-max notice); a couple of JS/Python pages with images missing alt
Roll-up Average score 97.8 across 8 pages; no broken internal links in the sample

That mix is the point of the exercise. A homepage that scores 100 can still sit next to a blog index with a long title and no H1. A useful mini auditor shows both — still with a tiny crawl budget.

Step 1: be a polite bot

Identify yourself. The educational User-Agent in this tutorial is:

LindenwerkDataEducationalBot/0.1 (+https://dev.to/lindenwerkdata; educational tiny SEO site-audit tutorial; honours robots.txt)

Then honour RFC 9309-style robots rules with urllib.robotparser. The script fetches /robots.txt first (capped body size). Practical rules we use:

  • HTTP 404 / other 4xx on robots.txt → treat as no rules, allow the fetch (common convention; example.com returned 404 in our run and we continued).
  • HTTP 5xx on robots.txt → treat as disallow (conservative).
  • Otherwise parse the file and require both our bot name and User-agent: * to be allowed for the URL we are about to request.
  • Every later page and internal link check goes through the same parser.

On 6 November 2026, crawlee.dev and docs.python.org served normal robots files that allow / for * and our bot. A unit check of RobotFileParser with Disallow: / correctly returns False for /.

from urllib.parse import urlsplit, urlunsplit
from urllib.robotparser import RobotFileParser

def robots_allows(session, page_url):
    parts = urlsplit(page_url)
    robots_url = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, "/robots.txt", "", ""))
    r = session.get(robots_url, timeout=15, stream=True)
    # ... read a capped body ...
    if 400 <= r.status_code < 500:
        return True, f"robots.txt {r.status_code} (no rules → allow)"
    if r.status_code >= 500:
        return False, f"robots.txt {r.status_code} (treat as disallow)"
    rp = RobotFileParser()
    rp.parse(body.decode("utf-8", "replace").splitlines())
    target = urlunsplit((parts.scheme, parts.netloc, parts.path or "/", parts.query, ""))
    allowed = rp.can_fetch("LindenwerkDataEducationalBot", target) and rp.can_fetch("*", target)
    return allowed, "robots.txt OK"

If robots say no, the site row is stored as robots_disallowed and no HTML crawl is started.

Step 2: a tiny breadth-first crawl 

from collections import deque

queue = deque([(start_url, 0)])
seen = set()
while queue and len(pages) < max_pages:
    url, depth = queue.popleft()
    if url in seen:
        continue
    seen.add(url)
    if not robots_allows_url(robots, url):
        continue
    # GET with timeout + 1 MB body cap, then parse …
    if depth < max_depth:
        for href in internal_hrefs:
            queue.append((href, depth + 1))

Defaults in the script: 10 pages, depth 2, 0.75 s pause between requests, 15 s timeout, 1 MB HTML cap. Query strings are stripped when discovering new URLs (keeps the frontier small). Static asset extensions (.png, .css, .js, …) are skipped. mailto: and tel: are never followed.

Live on 6 November 2026 with --max-pages 8 --max-depth 2:

  • example.com → 1 page (no further internal links)
  • crawlee.dev → 8 pages
  • docs.python.org → 8 pages
  • httpbin.org → 2 pages

Step 3: per-page on-page checks

An HTMLParser subclass collects </code>, meta tags, H1 count, <code>rel=canonical</code>, Open Graph keys, image <code>alt</code> presence and anchor <code>href</code>s — without walking <code>mailto:</code> / <code>tel:</code>.</p> <p>For each page the script records:</p> <div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table> <thead> <tr> <th>Signal</th> <th>How we treat it (educational soft targets)</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>HTTP status / redirects</td> <td>4xx/5xx = error; ≥2 redirect hops = warning</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Title length</td> <td>missing = error; < 30 = warning; > 60 = notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Meta description</td> <td>missing = warning; outside ~70–160 = notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td>H1</td> <td>0 = warning; > 1 = notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Canonical</td> <td>missing = notice; cross-domain = warning; self vs other labelled</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Indexability</td> <td> <code>noindex</code> in meta robots or <code>X-Robots-Tag</code> = warning</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Open Graph</td> <td>no <code>og:title</code> / <code>og:description</code> / <code>og:image</code> / <code>og:url</code> = notice</td> </tr> <tr> <td>Images</td> <td>count of <code><img></code> with missing/empty <code>alt</code> </td> </tr> </tbody> </table></div> <p><code>example.com</code> on 6 November 2026 is a useful teaching case. The live HTML is a short documentation stub: title <strong>"Example Domain"</strong> (14 characters), <strong>no H1</strong>, no meta description, no canonical, no Open Graph. Score <strong>86</strong>. (Older textbook copies of that page had an H1 — the public page changed; the script reports what the network returns today.)</p> <p><code>crawlee.dev/</code> scored <strong>100</strong> on the same day: title 40 chars, description 146, one H1, self-canonical, Open Graph keys present, 14 images all with alt text.</p> <h2> Step 4: a few broken internal links only </h2> <p>Full-site link checking is expensive and easy to abuse. The educational script keeps a small pool of internal URLs discovered during the crawl that were <strong>not</strong> already fetched as pages, then:</p> <ol> <li>skips any URL robots disallow,</li> <li>sends <strong>HEAD</strong> (falls back to a tiny GET if the host rejects HEAD),</li> <li>stops after <code>--max-link-checks</code> (default 15).</li> </ol> <p>Broken samples land on the site row as <code>broken_internal_links</code> and contribute a site-level <code>broken_internal_link</code> issue. On our 6 November 2026 runs across example.com, crawlee.dev, docs.python.org, httpbin.org and cloudflare.com, the sampled internal links all responded OK — which is a fine outcome; the plumbing is what you are learning.</p> <h2> Step 5: read AI-bot rules (do not wear their badges) </h2> <p>Many sites now name AI crawlers explicitly in <code>robots.txt</code>. The script looks for a short list (GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, OAI-SearchBot, ClaudeBot, Anthropic-AI, Claude-Web, Google-Extended, PerplexityBot, CCBot, …) and, for each:</p> <ul> <li>whether the name appears in the file,</li> <li>whether <code>RobotFileParser.can_fetch(bot_name, homepage)</code> is true,</li> <li>a one-line policy hint.</li> </ul> <p><strong>Important:</strong> page fetches and link checks always use <em>our</em> educational User-Agent. We never send <code>User-Agent: GPTBot</code> to "see what the CDN does". Impersonating another bot is rude, often against terms, and unnecessary for reading a public rules file.</p> <p>On 6 November 2026, <code>cloudflare.com/robots.txt</code> explicitly named GPTBot, ChatGPT-User, Google-Extended, Anthropic-AI, Claude-Web, CCBot, PerplexityBot (and Cohere-ai) with <code>Allow: /</code> for each. The script reported <code>named_in_robots: true</code> and <code>homepage_allowed: true</code> for those entries. <code>crawlee.dev</code> and <code>docs.python.org</code> named none of the AI bots in our teaching list — they fall under <code>User-agent: *</code>.</p> <h2> Step 6: optional <code>llms.txt</code> and sitemap presence </h2> <p>Two cheap HEAD/GET probes (still rate-limited):</p> <ul> <li> <code>/llms.txt</code> — present or not (reported as information; search engines may ignore it).</li> <li>Sitemap — first <code>Sitemap:</code> URL from robots.txt, else <code>/sitemap.xml</code>.</li> </ul> <p>Live on 6 November 2026:</p> <div class="table-wrapper-paragraph"><table> <thead> <tr> <th>Site</th> <th>Sitemap</th> <th>llms.txt</th> </tr> </thead> <tbody> <tr> <td>example.com</td> <td>404</td> <td>404</td> </tr> <tr> <td>crawlee.dev</td> <td>200 (from robots)</td> <td>200</td> </tr> <tr> <td>docs.python.org</td> <td>200 (from robots)</td> <td>404</td> </tr> <tr> <td>httpbin.org</td> <td>404</td> <td>404</td> </tr> <tr> <td>cloudflare.com</td> <td>200 (from robots)</td> <td>200</td> </tr> </tbody> </table></div> <h2> Step 7: score, fix hints, CSV and JSON </h2> <p>Each page starts at <strong>100</strong>. Unique issue ids subtract <strong>10</strong> (error), <strong>4</strong> (warning) or <strong>1</strong> (notice). Every issue carries a short <code>fix</code> string a non-engineer can read:<br /> </p> <div class="highlight js-code-highlight"> <pre class="highlight json"><code><span class="p">{</span> <span class="nl">"id"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="s2">"title_short"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nl">"severity"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="s2">"warning"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nl">"message"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="s2">"Title only 14 chars (soft min ~30)"</span><span class="p">,</span> <span class="nl">"fix"</span><span class="p">:</span> <span class="s2">"Expand the title toward ~30–60 characters without stuffing."</span> <span class="p">}</span> </code></pre> </div> <p>Outputs:</p> <ul> <li> <strong>JSON</strong> — site row (<code>rowType: "site"</code>) plus one page row per URL (<code>rowType: "page"</code>), including the AI-bot matrix and broken-link samples.</li> <li> <strong>CSV</strong> — flat spreadsheet of page metrics plus a <code>[site]</code> summary row with average score and top issue ids.</li> </ul> <p>Soft length targets are teaching defaults, not Google policy quotes. Adjust them for your own style guide.</p> <h2> Limitations you should expect </h2> <ol> <li> <strong>Client-rendered apps</strong> may ship an almost empty HTML shell. A single GET will under-count H1s and text. Headless browsers are out of scope here on purpose.</li> <li> <strong>Soft title/description ranges</strong> are conventions, not guarantees of ranking.</li> <li> <strong>Broken-link sample ≠ full link audit.</strong> Raising <code>--max-link-checks</code> still only samples the frontier; it is not a substitute for a dedicated checker.</li> <li> <strong>AI-bot matrix is a reading aid.</strong> Bot names change; keep the list short and honest.</li> <li> <strong>The rule list is tiny.</strong> Real auditors have dozens of rule types (hreflang, JSON-LD, thin content, mixed content, …). Growing yours is fine — keep evidence, keep caps, keep robots.</li> </ol> <h2> Scheduling a weekly re-audit </h2> <p>Companion file <code>crontab.txt</code>:<br /> </p> <div class="highlight js-code-highlight"> <pre class="highlight plaintext"><code>CRON_TZ=Europe/Berlin 30 7 * * 1 cd /path/to/code && ./venv/bin/python seo_audit.py -f domains.txt --max-pages 10 --max-depth 2 --out-dir out >> out/cron.log 2>&1 </code></pre> </div> <p>Keep <code>max-pages</code> low. A free shared runner is not a reason to hammer strangers. Diff this week's JSON against last week's if you want a change watch — the educational script itself does not ship a state file (unlike a one-page tech detector); a <code>jq</code> diff is enough to start.</p> <h2> Live results (6 November 2026) </h2> <p>Fresh venv, Python 3.13.5, <code>requests</code> 2.32.4. The script never parses <code>mailto:</code> / <code>tel:</code> and never posts forms.</p> <h2> Run it yourself </h2> <div class="highlight js-code-highlight"> <pre class="highlight shell"><code>python3 -m venv venv ./venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt <span class="c"># pins requests</span> ./venv/bin/python seo_audit.py \ example.com crawlee.dev docs.python.org \ --max-pages 10 --max-depth 2 --out-dir out </code></pre> </div> <p>Useful flags: <code>--max-link-checks 15</code>, <code>--no-llms</code>, <code>--no-sitemap</code>, <code>--file domains.txt</code>, <code>--pause 1.0</code>. An example <code>crontab.txt</code> in the companion folder shows a Monday weekly re-audit; it is not installed for you.</p> <h2> Where to take it next </h2> <ul> <li>Feed a CSV of <em>your own</em> sites or client domains and keep the pause (or slower).</li> <li>Raise caps only when you have permission and a reason.</li> <li>Add duplicate-title detection across the small page set you already fetched.</li> <li>Add security-header scoring (HSTS, CSP) as a separate optional block.</li> <li>Export the issues array into a spreadsheet your editor can tick through.</li> <li>For agency lead lists, start from domains you are allowed to review — do not scrape personal contact details to build those lists.</li> </ul> <p>Still a tiny crawl. Still no personal data. Still your script, under your control.</p> <h2> Privacy checklist (short) </h2> <p>Before you point this at someone else's property in bulk:</p> <ol> <li>You have a legitimate reason (your inventory, a client who asked, research you are allowed to do).</li> <li>robots.txt is honoured; a clear bot name is in the User-Agent; requests are rate-limited.</li> <li>Outputs are scanned for e-mails and phone numbers (our live runs: <strong>zero</strong>).</li> <li>Form posts, account areas, <code>mailto:</code> / <code>tel:</code> and cookie <strong>values</strong> are off limits.</li> <li>AI-bot names are read from robots.txt — never sent as the request User-Agent.</li> <li>Soft SEO scores are not sold as a ranking certificate.</li> </ol> <p>That checklist is operational hygiene, not legal advice.</p> <h2> Terms and honesty </h2> <p>Only public HTML, headers and robots.txt are used. Honour robots.txt and site terms. Do not use this pattern to build bulk marketing lists of people. Vendor and bot names (Google, OpenAI, Anthropic, Cloudflare, …) are used as factual labels for publicly visible rules and pages; this tutorial is independent and not affiliated with or endorsed by those organisations. title: Your AI agent found a new IBAN on an invoice. Should it pay? (IBAN checks in Python, and their limits)
summary:
An invoice arrives. Same supplier, same amount pattern, but the IBAN is different. If an AI agent prepares your payments, what should it do?

Bank-detail changes are a classic invoice-fraud pattern, and agents make it more interesting: they read every PDF, never get tired and will happily "fix" vendor master data if the instructions say so. So I tested what an IBAN check actually catches.

Disclosure: I built the IBAN Validator & Bank Lookup on Apify, which I use below. The lesson applies to any validator.

The test

Nine inputs: a known-good German IBAN, the same IBAN with one typo, three IBANs where I changed the account number and recomputed the two check digits (what a fraudster would do), plus Dutch, French, Austrian and a truncated one.

import os, requests

URL = ("https://api.apify.com/v2/acts/fast_data_asap~iban-validator-bank-lookup"
       "/run-sync-get-dataset-items")
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['APIFY_TOKEN']}"}

ibans = [
    "DE89370400440532013000",        # original
    "DE89 3704 0044 0532 0130 01",   # one digit typo
    "DE62370400440532013001",        # changed account + recomputed check digits
    "DE40370400440532013009",
    "DE18370400440532013017",
    "NL91ABNA0417164300", "FR1420041010050500013M02606", "AT611904300234573201",
    "DE12345",
]
resp = requests.post(URL, headers=HEADERS, timeout=120,
                     json={"ibans": ibans, "includeBankInfo": True})
resp.raise_for_status()
for r in resp.json():
    print(r["input"], r["valid"], r["checksumValid"], r["nationalChecksumValid"], r["bankName"], r["error"])

The result

Input Valid MOD-97 National check Bank
DE89 …013000 (original) yes ok ok Commerzbank
DE89 …013001 (typo) no fails ok Commerzbank
DE62 …013001 (changed, recomputed) yes ok ok Commerzbank
DE40 …013009 (changed, recomputed) yes ok ok Commerzbank
DE18 …013017 (changed, recomputed) yes ok ok Commerzbank
NL91 ABNA… yes ok – ABN AMRO
FR14 2004… yes ok ok La Banque Postale
AT61 1904… yes ok – (no bank data)
DE12345 no fails – wrong length

Real output, run on 12 November 2026. Malformed rows are not charged.

Two takeaways:

  1. Typos are caught. The IBAN check digits (ISO 7064 MOD-97) exist exactly for that, and the one-digit typo fails.
  2. Deliberate changes are not. Recompute the two check digits and the IBAN is mathematically perfect. For these three accounts the German national account check passed as well. To every format rule, a fraudulent IBAN at the same bank looks exactly like a real one.

A validator answers "is this a well-formed IBAN, and which bank is it?". It cannot answer "does this account belong to my supplier?".

What the validator is good for in an agent

The useful signal is not valid, it is the comparison with what you already know:

Signal Source What the agent should do
valid: false validator reject, ask for corrected invoice
IBAN differs from vendor master data your ERP hold payment, never update master data automatically
bankName / bic differs from the known bank validator + ERP hold, flag as high risk
country of the bank differs from the supplier's country validator + ERP hold, flag as high risk
new IBAN confirmed by the supplier through a known channel human release

Here is that rule as code:

def iban_decision(invoice_iban: str, vendor: dict, check: dict) -> tuple[str, str]:
    """vendor = your master data, check = one row from the validator."""
    if not check["valid"]:
        return "reject", check["error"]
    if check["iban"].replace(" ", "") == vendor["iban"].replace(" ", ""):
        return "pay", "IBAN matches master data"
    reasons = ["IBAN differs from master data"]
    if check.get("bic") and vendor.get("bic") and check["bic"][:8] != vendor["bic"][:8]:
        reasons.append(f"bank changed: {vendor.get('bank')} -> {check.get('bankName')}")
    if check["countryCode"] != vendor["iban"][:2]:
        reasons.append("bank country changed")
    return "hold", "; ".join(reasons) + " - confirm with supplier via known phone number"

The important design choice: the agent can never move from "hold" to "pay" on its own. It can prepare the evidence (old vs new bank, invoice, sender address), but the release needs a human or a bank-side confirmation.

Verification of Payee does the part a validator cannot

Since October 2025, EU payment service providers have to offer Verification of Payee for euro credit transfers: before you send money, your bank checks whether the payee name matches the account holder of that IBAN and tells you "match", "close match" or "no match". That is the check that would expose the fraudulent IBANs above, because the name on the account would not be your supplier's.

So the full chain for an accounts-payable agent looks like this:

  1. Format and bank (validator): cheap, offline, catches typos and tells you which bank.
  2. Master-data comparison (your system): catches changes.
  3. Verification of Payee (your bank, at payment time): catches wrong account holders.
  4. Human release for every change.

Try it

IBAN Validator & Bank Lookup on Apify: bulk IBAN validation with MOD-97 and national checksums, SEPA flag, bank name and BIC (German banks from the Bundesbank file), $0.0005 per IBAN, runs offline inside the actor. For the full supplier check (company register, VAT ID, IBAN) see our free Agent Skill verify-supplier-de.

This is about payment hygiene, not legal advice.

Question: if you let an agent prepare payments, where do you draw the line: may it ever update vendor bank details, or is that always a human step?

title: ¿Por qué osFoundry obliga a Claude a indicar la pestaña de Slides exacta y a usar una clave en cada cita?
summary:
Esta es la llamada de creación que recibe una conexión de Claude para las Notes de osFoundry. Se obtuvo con un tools/list sin autenticar contra el endpoint MCP público el 2026-11-09 y está recortada:

{"name": "create_note_tab",
 "description": "Create a new Slides or Sheet tab in an approved Note. Use the version from list_note_tabs; returns the exact new tab ID for later edits. An optional outline fills a Slides tab. A repeated idempotency key returns the first tab.",
 "inputSchema": {
   "required": ["note_id", "expected_version", "idempotency_key", "tab_type"],
   "properties": {
     "tab_type": {"enum": ["slides", "sheet"]},
     "label": {"type": "string"},
     "slides": {"type": "array", "minItems": 1, "maxItems": 20,
                "items": {"required": ["title"], "additionalProperties": false,
                          "properties": {"title": {}, "body": {}, "notes": {}}}}},
   "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:write"]}]}

Sus dos vecinas para este trabajo:

{"name": "add_note_source",
 "description": "Add an HTTP or HTTPS citation to the Sources tab of an approved Note. Uses the Note version and an idempotency key; returns the new source ID.",
 "inputSchema": {"required": ["note_id", "expected_version", "idempotency_key", "title", "url"]}}

{"name": "list_note_tabs",
 "description": "List every tab instance and its type. A Note may have multiple Slides or Sheet tabs; use the exact tab ID returned here."}

Tres frases sostienen el diseño: "every tab instance", "returns the exact new tab ID" y "a repeated idempotency key returns the first". El resto del post reconstruye las herramientas en Python y mide qué evita cada una de esas frases. El bloqueo optimista sobre la versión de la Note es tema de otro post y aquí solo aparece donde interactúa con las otras dos.

¿Qué puede poner Claude realmente en una diapositiva?

Menos que el asistente propio de la app de escritorio. Dentro de osFoundry, slide_create_deck_from_outline y slide_add_slide del asistente de Notes (en apps/web/src/screens/notes/lib/note-surface-tools.ts) aceptan layouts, viñetas, contenido a dos columnas, tablas, imágenes y uno de cinco temas. El elemento de outline del conector es title, body, notes, con additionalProperties: false. edit_note_tab ofrece slide_add para una diapositiva y slides_add_outline para un array, ambos con los mismos tres campos.

code/note_store.py carga la respuesta guardada de tools/list y valida los payloads contra ella con un validador mínimo (required, enum, additionalProperties, minItems/maxItems). Ocho payloads que un modelo podría enviar perfectamente:

edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slide_add", "title": "Sources", "body": "3 links"}  -> ok
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slide_add", "title": "Sources", "index": 0}         -> unexpected index
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slides_add", "slides": [{"title": "a"}]}            -> operation: not in enum
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slides_add_outline", "slides": [{... "bullets"}]}   -> slides: [0] unexpected bullets
create_note_tab  {"tab_type": "slides", "slides": "[21 items]"}                     -> slides: maxItems 20
create_note_tab  {"tab_type": "markdown"}                                           -> tab_type: not in enum
add_note_source  {"url": "https://example.org/report"}                              -> missing title
list_note_attachments {"kind": "sources", "limit": 100}                             -> ok

El último pasa este validador, pero no el esquema real completo: limit tiene maximum: 50, y la reconstrucción no lo comprueba. slide_add no puede elegir posición, create_note_tab no puede crear una pestaña Markdown y un deck de más de 20 diapositivas necesita más de una llamada. Un esquema estrecho es una decisión sobre quién da estilo al deck: el conector escribe el contenido y una persona en la app de escritorio aplica temas y layout.

¿Por qué un ID de pestaña exacto y no "la pestaña de slides"?

Porque la propia app de escritorio sigue aceptando el atajo, y el atajo elige la primera coincidencia. resolveTabInstanceId() en apps/web/src/screens/notes/types.ts:

if (cfg.some((t) => t.id === rawTabId)) return rawTabId
const byType = cfg.find((t) => t.type === rawTabId)
if (byType) return byType.id

Ese fallback mantiene funcionando enlaces antiguos como …/slides. Para un agente significa que "editar slides" va a parar a la pestaña de Slides que esté primero en la barra. Las pestañas nuevas reciben IDs como slides-9-mh8z1k2a de nextTabId() en NotesContentPanel.tsx, las fijas son markdown, files y sources, y una persona puede añadir tantas pestañas de Slides como quiera, arrastrarlas a otro orden y renombrarlas, incluso con nombres repetidos (handleRename solo hace trim).

La reconstrucción le da a una Note K pestañas de Slides con etiquetas distintas. Un agente scriptado lista las pestañas, elige un deck como objetivo y guarda una referencia a él: su posición en la barra, su tipo, su etiqueta o su ID. Entre turnos del agente, la persona hace de cero a dos cambios aleatorios (mover una pestaña 40%, renombrar una pestaña de Slides con una de las cinco etiquetas 35%, añadir una pestaña de Slides 25%). Después el agente vuelve a listar y resuelve su referencia. 10,000 pruebas por K, seed 7:

K decks referencia correcto deck equivocado no encontrado
2 posición 83.7% 16.3% 0.0%
2 tipo 50.7% 49.3% 0.0%
2 etiqueta 85.6% 2.1% 12.3%
2 ID 100% 0 0
5 posición 82.7% 17.3% 0.0%
5 tipo 19.7% 80.3% 0.0%
5 etiqueta 92.1% 3.0% 5.0%
5 ID 100% 0 0

La referencia por tipo acierta 1/K de las veces, como era de esperar. La posición falla cada vez que un arrastre cruza el objetivo, sea cual sea K. La etiqueta es la tentadora, porque es lo que la persona escribe en el prompt, y acierta la mayoría de las veces. El 2–3% en que falla son los casos malos: otro deck lleva ahora esa etiqueta y el agente escribe en él sin ningún error. "No encontrado" es el fallo seguro. Un ID se asigna una vez y nunca se reutiliza, así que sobrevive a cualquier cambio que la persona pueda hacer en la barra de pestañas.

¿La comprobación de versión no detecta ya una pestaña equivocada?

No. Cada cambio en la barra de pestañas de los de arriba incrementa la versión de la Note, así que una escritura obsoleta se rechaza y el agente vuelve a listar. El nuevo listado le da una versión actual, y entonces resuelve su referencia antigua contra la lista nueva. el servidor comprueba política de clave del cliente pestañas creadas (llamadas enviadas)
clave, luego versión clave nueva por llamada 63 (76) / 75 (100) / 62 (74)
clave, luego versión misma clave al reintentar 50 (67) / 50 (81) / 50 (62)
clave, luego versión clave nueva tras un conflicto 50 (67) / 50 (81) / 50 (62)
versión, luego clave clave nueva por llamada 63 (76) / 75 (100) / 62 (74)

hash de la URL tal como está escrita 4,814 2,452 8.17

event_model_payload.headline: ¿Por qué osFoundry obliga a Claude a indicar la pestaña de Slides exacta y a usar una clave en cada cita?
event_model_payload.summary:
Esta es la llamada de creación que recibe una conexión de Claude para las Notes de osFoundry. Se obtuvo con un tools/list sin autenticar contra el endpoint MCP público el 2026-11-09 y está recortada:

{"name": "create_note_tab",
 "description": "Create a new Slides or Sheet tab in an approved Note. Use the version from list_note_tabs; returns the exact new tab ID for later edits. An optional outline fills a Slides tab. A repeated idempotency key returns the first tab.",
 "inputSchema": {
   "required": ["note_id", "expected_version", "idempotency_key", "tab_type"],
   "properties": {
     "tab_type": {"enum": ["slides", "sheet"]},
     "label": {"type": "string"},
     "slides": {"type": "array", "minItems": 1, "maxItems": 20,
                "items": {"required": ["title"], "additionalProperties": false,
                          "properties": {"title": {}, "body": {}, "notes": {}}}}},
   "additionalProperties": false},
 "annotations": {"readOnlyHint": false, "destructiveHint": true},
 "securitySchemes": [{"type": "oauth2", "scopes": ["osfoundry:write"]}]}

Sus dos vecinas para este trabajo:

{"name": "add_note_source",
 "description": "Add an HTTP or HTTPS citation to the Sources tab of an approved Note. Uses the Note version and an idempotency key; returns the new source ID.",
 "inputSchema": {"required": ["note_id", "expected_version", "idempotency_key", "title", "url"]}}

{"name": "list_note_tabs",
 "description": "List every tab instance and its type. A Note may have multiple Slides or Sheet tabs; use the exact tab ID returned here."}

Tres frases sostienen el diseño: "every tab instance", "returns the exact new tab ID" y "a repeated idempotency key returns the first". El resto del post reconstruye las herramientas en Python y mide qué evita cada una de esas frases. El bloqueo optimista sobre la versión de la Note es tema de otro post y aquí solo aparece donde interactúa con las otras dos.

¿Qué puede poner Claude realmente en una diapositiva?

Menos que el asistente propio de la app de escritorio. Dentro de osFoundry, slide_create_deck_from_outline y slide_add_slide del asistente de Notes (en apps/web/src/screens/notes/lib/note-surface-tools.ts) aceptan layouts, viñetas, contenido a dos columnas, tablas, imágenes y uno de cinco temas. El elemento de outline del conector es title, body, notes, con additionalProperties: false. edit_note_tab ofrece slide_add para una diapositiva y slides_add_outline para un array, ambos con los mismos tres campos.

code/note_store.py carga la respuesta guardada de tools/list y valida los payloads contra ella con un validador mínimo (required, enum, additionalProperties, minItems/maxItems). Ocho payloads que un modelo podría enviar perfectamente:

edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slide_add", "title": "Sources", "body": "3 links"}  -> ok
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slide_add", "title": "Sources", "index": 0}         -> unexpected index
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slides_add", "slides": [{"title": "a"}]}            -> operation: not in enum
edit_note_tab    {"operation": "slides_add_outline", "slides": [{... "bullets"}]}   -> slides: [0] unexpected bullets
create_note_tab  {"tab_type": "slides", "slides": "[21 items]"}                     -> slides: maxItems 20
create_note_tab  {"tab_type": "markdown"}                                           -> tab_type: not in enum
add_note_source  {"url": "https://example.org/report"}                              -> missing title
list_note_attachments {"kind": "sources", "limit": 100}                             -> ok

El último pasa este validador, pero no el esquema real completo: limit tiene maximum: 50, y la reconstrucción no lo comprueba. slide_add no puede elegir posición, create_note_tab no puede crear una pestaña Markdown y un deck de más de 20 diapositivas necesita más de una llamada. Un esquema estrecho es una decisión sobre quién da estilo al deck: el conector escribe el contenido y una persona en la app de escritorio aplica temas y layout.

Porque la propia app de escritorio sigue aceptando el atajo, y el atajo elige la primera coincidencia. resolveTabInstanceId() en apps/web/src/screens/notes/types.ts:

if (cfg.some((t) => t.id === rawTabId)) return rawTabId
const byType = cfg.find((t) => t.type === rawTabId)
if (byType) return byType.id

Ese fallback mantiene funcionando enlaces antiguos como …/slides. Para un agente significa que "editar slides" va a parar a la pestaña de Slides que esté primero en la barra. 2 tipo 50.7% 49.3% 0.0%
2 etiqueta 85.6% 2.1% 12.3%
2 ID 100% 0 0
5 posición 82.7% 17.3% 0.0%
5 tipo 19.7% 80.3% 0.0%
5 etiqueta 92.1% 3.0% 5.0%
5 ID 100% 0 0

title: How to merge Shift_JIS, UTF-8 BOM, and Windows-1252 CSVs without guessing the encoding
summary:
How to merge Shift_JIS, UTF-8 BOM, and Windows-1252 CSVs without guessing the encoding

A shop export from Japan, another from the UK, a third from a US system, and a Chinese marketplace file. You want one table. pandas.read_csv() with the default UTF-8 encoding fails on three of the four files. Dates arrive as 2026/3/2, 20260310, 2026年3月14日, and 3/15/2026. Two rows are exact duplicates, one row is empty, and one amount is written in full-width digits (２４９).

This article walks through that exact problem using sheetstack-lite, a small MIT-licensed Python tool. Every command below was run against the repository's fictional sample files. The output is copied from those runs, not reconstructed from memory.

sheetstack-lite is a free, in-memory merge-and-clean utility. It is not a tax tool, and this article does not claim compatibility with Google Sheets or WPS.

What the sample files actually contain

Clone the repo and install the two dependencies (pandas and openpyxl). Python 3.10 or later is required.

git clone https://github.com/ebhow9986-ctrl/sheetstack-lite.git
cd sheetstack-lite
python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate   # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install -r requirements.txt

The samples/ folder ships with five fictional CSVs (none of the rows are real customer records):

File What the tool reported What is messy about it
store_us.csv utf-8-sig (UTF-8 with a BOM) Mixed date formats, a blank row, a duplicate US-1002
store_uk.csv cp1252 The word “Café” is a single 0xE9 byte; one date is 3/6/2026; UK-2003 is duplicated
store_jp.csv shift_jis Japanese headers (伝票番号, 日付, 商品名…); dates such as 2026年3月14日 and 20260310; JP-3005 is duplicated
store_cn.csv gb18030 Chinese headers; a full-width amount ２４９; a date written as 2026年3月13日
customers_messy.csv utf-8-sig Duplicate ids, an empty row, mixed dates, a full-width ０８ in the points column

The README describes the four store files as “GBK” for the Chinese export. When the CLI sniffed the same file, it printed gb18030 (a superset of GBK). The rest of this article uses the string the tool actually printed.

Why a default pandas read fails

On the same machine, pd.read_csv(path) with no encoding= argument succeeded only for the UTF-8 BOM file. The other three store exports raised UnicodeDecodeError:

store_cn.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xb6 in position 0: invalid start byte
store_jp.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0x93 in position 0: invalid start byte
store_uk.csv: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte 0xe9 in position 67: invalid continuation byte

That last one is the é in “Café”. If you force latin-1 or cp1252 onto the Japanese file, the read may “succeed” and give you mojibake instead of an error. Encoding has to be chosen per file, then the headers have to be lined up, then the dates and duplicates have to be cleaned. Doing that by hand for every export is the tedious part.

This is a well-worn problem — the Stack Overflow thread “UnicodeDecodeError when reading CSV file in Pandas” has been viewed more than a million times. The usual advice is “pass encoding=...”. That works when you already know the encoding and you only have one file. It does not merge four different code pages, or rename 伝票番号 and Order ID into the same column.

Merge the four store exports

The tool is invoked as python3 sheetstack_lite.py. Two subcommands exist: merge and clean.

Point merge at the four store files, ask it to normalize header aliases, and write a single CSV:

python3 sheetstack_lite.py merge \
  samples/store_us.csv \
  samples/store_uk.csv \
  samples/store_jp.csv \
  samples/store_cn.csv \
  -o stores.csv \
  --normalize-headers

Exact output from the run:

Merged 4 file(s), 21 rows, 7 columns
  - store_us.csv: 7 rows / encoding utf-8-sig
  - store_uk.csv: 5 rows / encoding cp1252
  - store_jp.csv: 6 rows / encoding shift_jis
  - store_cn.csv: 3 rows / encoding gb18030
Wrote stores.csv

--normalize-headers maps common aliases onto one English name. In these samples that means, among others:

  • Order ID / 伝票番号 / 订单编号 → order_id
  • Date / 日付 / 成交时间 → order_date
  • Item / 商品名 / 商品名称 → product
  • Quantity / 数量 / 件数 → qty
  • Sales / 売上 / 销售额 → amount
  • Remaining / 在庫 / 库存数 → stock

A source_file column is added unless you pass --no-source. The merged file still has 21 rows, including the blank US row and the three duplicate orders. Dates are not rewritten during merge. “Café mug”, スマホスタンド, and 键盘 all sit in the same product column, and the file is written as UTF-8 with a BOM (utf-8-sig) so Excel on Windows will not treat the CJK text as mojibake.

A shop export from Japan, another from the UK, a third from a US system, and a Chinese marketplace file. You want one table. pandas.read_csv() with the default UTF-8 encoding fails on three of the four files. Dates arrive as 2026/3/2, 20260310, 2026年3月14日, and 3/15/2026. pip install -r requirements.txt

title: How to Debug an Old noindex Verdict in Google Search Console
summary:
You publish a site migration and open a guide at its expected address. It loads. Google Search Console still shows that a crawler found a noindex tag. Before changing the deployment again, check when Google fetched the URL and what the public server sends today.

A noindex directive can come from the HTML or the HTTP headers. A stored indexing report can reflect an older response. Comparing the two versions gives you a specific next action.

Check the first public response

Use the exact URL you want readers to find, including the scheme, host and trailing slash. Save the following script as check_noindex.py. It performs one GET and stops at a redirect so you can see the first status and its Location header.

import argparse
from html.parser import HTMLParser
from urllib.error import HTTPError, URLError
from urllib.parse import urlsplit
from urllib.request import HTTPRedirectHandler, Request, build_opener


class NoRedirect(HTTPRedirectHandler):
    def redirect_request(self, req, fp, code, msg, headers, newurl):
        return None


class PageMetadata(HTMLParser):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.in_head = False
        self.canonicals = []
        self.robots = []

    def handle_starttag(self, tag, attrs):
        fields = dict(attrs)
        if tag == "head":
            self.in_head = True
        if tag == "meta":
            name = (fields.get("name") or "").lower()
            if name in {"robots", "googlebot", "googlebot-news"}:
                self.robots.append((name, fields.get("content") or ""))
        rel = (fields.get("rel") or "").lower().split()
        if self.in_head and tag == "link" and "canonical" in rel:
            self.canonicals.append(fields.get("href") or "")

    def handle_endtag(self, tag):
        if tag == "head":
            self.in_head = False


def inspect(url):
    target = urlsplit(url)
    if target.scheme not in {"http", "https"} or not target.hostname:
        raise SystemExit("Enter an HTTP or HTTPS URL.")

    opener = build_opener(NoRedirect)
    try:
        request = Request(url, headers={"Accept-Encoding": "identity"})
        response = opener.open(request, timeout=12)
    except HTTPError as error:
        response = error
    except (URLError, TimeoutError) as error:
        raise SystemExit(f"GET failed: {error}") from error

    with response:
        print(f"GET {response.geturl()} -> {response.status}")
        for name in ("Location", "Content-Type", "Content-Encoding", "X-Robots-Tag", "Link"):
            for value in response.headers.get_all(name, []):
                print(f"{name}: {value}")
        if response.status != 200:
            raise SystemExit("Inspect the status or destination before reading metadata.")
        if response.headers.get_content_type() != "text/html":
            raise SystemExit("Response is not HTML.")
        encodings = response.headers.get_all("Content-Encoding", [])
        if any(value.strip().lower() != "identity" for value in encodings):
            raise SystemExit("Decode the response body before inspecting its HTML.")
        limit = 2_000_000
        body = response.read(limit + 1)
        if len(body) > limit:
            raise SystemExit("HTML exceeds the example's 2 MB inspection limit.")
        page = PageMetadata()
        encoding = response.headers.get_content_charset() or "utf-8"
        page.feed(body.decode(encoding, errors="replace"))
        print(f"Canonical links in head: {page.canonicals}")
        print(f"Robots meta tags: {page.robots}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="Show one public HTML response's indexing signals.")
    parser.add_argument("url")
    inspect(parser.parse_args().url)

Run it first on your preferred URL.

python3 check_noindex.py https://example.com/guides/import/

The probe requests an uncompressed response and prints any Content-Encoding header it receives. If a server still sends gzip or Brotli, decode the body before inspecting the HTML. Reading compressed bytes as text can make a page with a noindex tag appear to have no robots meta tags. HTTP content coding

An HTTP 200 can carry both an HTML index, follow tag and an HTTP header such as X-Robots-Tag: googlebot: noindex. That header applies to Google’s main web crawler. Inspect every header and meta tag that applies to your search surface. A none directive also includes noindex. Google's robots tag reference

On a redirect, confirm the first hop, then run the same check on the intended destination. For HTML 200 responses, check the canonical in the document head. If the page also declares a canonical in an HTTP Link header, verify that both signals point to the same preferred URL. The script reports the directives it sees for this one request. Google’s canonical URL guidance

Compare the stored crawl with a live test

In URL Inspection, record the last crawl, page fetch, and indexing allowed fields from the Google Index view. Then run Test live URL for the preferred address and check whether crawling and indexing are allowed there. The live test follows redirects. Check the first hop, then test the intended destination directly. URL Inspection documentation

What you find Next action
Crawl allowed? says No, while Indexing allowed? says Yes Check the robots.txt rule for the exact URL. If the URL belongs in search, correct the matching rule for that path and rerun the live test.
The current response still tells Googlebot noindex Find which layer supplied it. Check the HTML template for meta tags and the server or CDN for response headers. Fix the intended public route and test again.
The stored crawl predates the deployment, and the live test allows indexing Record the deployed version and the old crawl date. Use the existing sitemap and links to support discovery. Request recrawling for an important changed URL if appropriate, then wait for a new stored result.
Google reports a different selected canonical Compare the declared canonical, redirect destination, sitemap entry, and internal links. Decide which URL represents the page and make those signals agree.

Read Crawl allowed? first. When robots.txt blocks the fetch, URL Inspection can show Yes under Indexing allowed? because Google could not read the page’s directives. The public GET above can still succeed in that situation because it does not check robots.txt. Use the live test to confirm that crawling is allowed and the fetch succeeds before interpreting the indexing field. Google’s explanation of the inspection fields

A live test that allows indexing confirms the current response is eligible in the tool. Use the stored result to see whether Google has indexed that URL and which canonical it chose. Google says repeated requests for the same URL won’t make it crawl faster. Google’s recrawl guidance

Check the next stored crawl

In a synthetic UTC timeline, Google’s 09:00 crawl found noindex. The corrected route deployed at 10:00. At 10:10, the public GET returned HTTP 200 with the expected canonical, and Google’s live test allowed indexing. When a newer stored crawl appears, check Indexing allowed and Google-selected canonical. If that crawl still reports noindex, open View crawled page and compare its response headers and HTML with the public GET. Use the two capture times to trace which response supplied the directive.

For several URLs with the same issue, review the affected examples in Page indexing before using Validate fix. A submitted-sitemap filter limits validation to known affected URLs in that sitemap when you start it. Monitor the issue’s validation details and use URL Inspection for each priority URL’s stored indexing status. Google’s Page indexing report

Try a public example

On 11 November 2026, the October Sarv Blog archive returned HTTP 200, declared its own canonical, and sent no robots meta tag or X-Robots-Tag on the checked response. I work with Sarv. You can run the same command on the archive and record what the server returns today.

For your own release, keep three pieces of evidence together. Save the first HTTP response, the live test verdict, and the date of the stored Google crawl. Compare them again after Google records a newer crawl.

I used AI for research, drafting, and editing assistance.

title: UI20 Inspection Photos: Build an Idempotent Review Ledger in Python
summary:
An inspection team exports a folder twice because the first upload appeared to stall. Both transfers finish. The reviewer now sees twice as many rows, although the team visited the same assets. A second folder arrives with an unchanged filename but different bytes. One importer silently replaces the earlier file, including the image that somebody already accepted. The photo viewer works. The handoff record has lost the ability to say what was reviewed.

This tutorial builds a small SQLite ledger for an inspection team evaluating a UI20 aircraft configuration. The ledger runs after files have been delivered to the team. The UI20 aircraft listing identifies the product to discuss with a supplier. The manifest and all payload bytes below are synthetic, and the code assumes the team supplies its own capture identifiers. The example requires Python's standard library and no access to the aircraft.

Decide what must survive a second import

Start by asking what should happen when the same export is delivered under a different folder name. A successful second import should leave the same captures and reviews in the ledger. A file path is useful for finding a file in one transfer, but the receiver cannot assume that path survives archiving, renaming or copying through a different operating system. A filename can also be recycled by a camera or a person's export script.

Define the unit of work with a key such as job ID, required view ID and capture ID. The job separates deliveries for different work orders. The view identifies the evidence requested for a particular asset or inspection question. The capture identifies one attempt to supply that view. The team assigns those identifiers and records them in a manifest before sending files. A path in that manifest points to the bytes in the current delivery. It can change on another delivery without changing the key. If two assets each need a label photo, their view IDs should be distinct in the job requirements.

Give the bytes a separate identity

Hash the original byte stream with SHA-256. The digest lets the receiver detect byte-for-byte equality. Include the byte count for storage and inspection, and retain the original bytes somewhere the ledger can reference. A digest of a preview or an image decoded and saved again describes a different artifact. For example, a program that strips metadata from a photo creates a new byte sequence even when a person cannot see a difference in the displayed image. Store derived artifacts with their own digest and a reference to the source.

Two capture keys can point to the same digest. The ledger retains both keys and only needs one blob record for those bytes. That situation can occur when a sender attaches the same file to multiple manifest rows. It warrants a review of the assignment. The digest alone cannot tell whether the image is suitable evidence for either required view. Keeping the two identities separate allows the receiver to find repeated bytes without silently dropping work or counting duplicates as additional completed views.

Define the three import outcomes

An unseen capture key is a new capture. A known key with the same digest is a replay. A known key with a different digest is a conflict. Those outcomes can be checked without timestamps or filenames. In particular, a file marked newer by a transfer service could still be a renamed copy of an older image. The team's manifest contract should say who can issue a new capture ID and what the receiver should do with a conflict.

This example rejects the conflicting batch and leaves earlier committed imports and reviews available. In production, a receiver can place the batch and its manifest in quarantine and give a human the job, view and capture key together with both digests. The sender can explain which item the delivery intended to replace. A corrected capture gets its own ID or follows a documented amendment process. A policy that overwrites old rows during ingestion makes the correction look like the original bytes were never there.

Build the ledger in SQLite

The example stores a blob digest and size, a capture-to-blob association, and one decision for each reviewed capture. The fixture uses small byte strings as stand-ins for image files. It stores no original bytes in SQLite. For a real handoff, save them in durable storage, verify the hash computed from what was written, and keep the locator alongside the digest. Build that storage and reconciliation layer before depending on the database as an operational record.

The import does the inserts and the comparison inside one transaction. The capture insert can skip a key that already exists. The following query checks the digest stored under that key. If the bytes conflict, an exception rolls back the import, including any new blob rows from that batch. The review uses a conditional insert so that a request referring to a stale or missing digest cannot attach a decision to a different capture. Identical decisions can be replayed. Changing an accepted decision requires a separate revision process with its own record.

from dataclasses import dataclass
from hashlib import sha256
import sqlite3


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Capture:
    job_id: str
    view_id: str
    capture_id: str
    payload: bytes

    @property
    def key(self):
        return self.job_id, self.view_id, self.capture_id


def open_ledger():
    db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
    db.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    db.executescript("""
        CREATE TABLE blob (
            digest TEXT PRIMARY KEY NOT NULL,
            byte_count INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (byte_count >= 0)
        );
        CREATE TABLE capture (
            job_id TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(job_id) > 0),
            view_id TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(view_id) > 0),
            capture_id TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (length(capture_id) > 0),
            digest TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES blob(digest),
            PRIMARY KEY (job_id, view_id, capture_id)
        );
        CREATE TABLE review (
            job_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            view_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            capture_id TEXT NOT NULL,
            digest TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES blob(digest),
            decision TEXT NOT NULL CHECK (decision IN ('accepted', 'rejected')),
            PRIMARY KEY (job_id, view_id, capture_id),
            FOREIGN KEY (job_id, view_id, capture_id)
                REFERENCES capture(job_id, view_id, capture_id)
        );
    """)
    return db


def import_export(db, rows):
    with db:
        for row in rows:
            digest = sha256(row.payload).hexdigest()
            db.execute("""
                INSERT INTO blob VALUES (?, ?)
                ON CONFLICT(digest) DO NOTHING
            """, (digest, len(row.payload)))
            db.execute("""
                INSERT INTO capture VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)
                ON CONFLICT(job_id, view_id, capture_id) DO NOTHING
            """, (*row.key, digest))
            stored = db.execute("""
                SELECT digest FROM capture
                WHERE job_id = ? AND view_id = ? AND capture_id = ?
            """, row.key).fetchone()
            if stored != (digest,):
                raise ValueError(f"Conflicting bytes for capture {row.key}")


def record_review(db, key, expected_digest, decision):
    if decision not in {"accepted", "rejected"}:
        raise ValueError("Unsupported review decision")
    with db:
        db.execute("""
            INSERT INTO review
            SELECT job_id, view_id, capture_id, digest, ? FROM capture
            WHERE job_id = ? AND view_id = ? AND capture_id = ? AND digest = ?
            ON CONFLICT(job_id, view_id, capture_id) DO NOTHING
        """, (decision, *key, expected_digest))
        stored = db.execute("""
            SELECT digest, decision FROM review
            WHERE job_id = ? AND view_id = ? AND capture_id = ?
        """, key).fetchone()
        if stored != (expected_digest, decision):
            raise ValueError(f"Review target or decision conflicts for {key}")


def missing_views(db, job_id, required):
    accepted = db.execute("""
        SELECT DISTINCT view_id FROM review
        WHERE job_id = ? AND decision = 'accepted'
    """, (job_id,))
